bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean for a handful of criteria on one story; use full for a complex feature with many scenarios, edge cases, and quality attributes.
bundles.summary: Defines the conditions a user story must satisfy to be accepted, so "done" is verifiable and shared rather than left to interpretation.
bundles.title: Acceptance Criteria

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean for a straightforward decision; use full for an architecturally significant one with several options weighed and detailed consequences.
bundles.summary: Records one architecturally significant decision: the forces that made it necessary, the options genuinely considered, the option chosen, and the consequences accepted. Immutable once accepted; superseded by a new record rather than edited.
bundles.title: Architecture Decision Record

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean (summary, steps to reproduce, expected and actual behavior, environment and reproducibility) for anything a non-tester will fill in; this is the one artifact in the family written by support agents, salespeople and users, and every extra field costs you reports. Use full when the defect is tracked formally: a release gate reads its severity, ownership crosses teams, or the closed record is audit evidence. Full adds evidence, the severity and priority pair with owners named, the triage decision, and the resolution with its regression guard - and three of those four are filled in by someone other than the reporter, after filing.
bundles.summary: The document that gets one defect fixed by someone who was not there: what you did, what you expected, what happened instead, and where. Written as an anomaly report rather than a diagnosis, because at the moment of writing nobody yet knows whether the cause is a code flaw, a configuration, or a misunderstanding.
bundles.title: Bug Report

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean (purpose and audience, the KPI table, review and ownership) for one team to agree what it watches and act on it. Use full when the dashboard feeds governance, when multiple teams must agree what a metric means, or when someone other than the author builds it on a BI platform; full adds locked metric definitions (formula, inclusions/exclusions, data steward), layout and RAG thresholds, and data sources and refresh.
bundles.summary: The defined set of key performance indicators an organization watches to know whether it is making progress toward its objectives, plus the specification of how each is measured, targeted, owned, and reviewed. A standing governance instrument and a platform-agnostic dashboard definition (not a live BI tool) that survives Goodhart's Law and the vanity-metric trap by keeping metrics actionable, precisely defined, owned, and reviewed on a cadence.
bundles.title: KPI Dashboard

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean for a single feature or a one-pager; use full for a substantial product area that needs detailed scope, success metrics, and a rollout plan.
bundles.summary: Defines what to build, for whom, and why, with scope and success criteria, so a team can design and build the right thing.
bundles.title: Product Requirements Document

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean (Product Goal, ordered items, ordering rationale, refinement and readiness) for a single team with one clear goal; use full when multiple teams or stakeholders dispute the order, there are real cross-team dependencies, or the backlog is large enough to need an explicit prioritization framework and health metrics.
bundles.summary: The single, ordered, emergent list of work for a product, in service of a Product Goal: what the team might do next, sequenced so the most valuable and most informative work sits at the top. The tactical, output-focused counterpart to the roadmap, and the source the sprint backlog is drawn from.
bundles.title: Product Backlog

additional_formats.guidance: Reach for the one-pager when the problem is understood and the hard part is choosing where to compete. It opens with a winning aspiration and cascades through where to play, how to win, and the capabilities that requires, so the argument is about the choice rather than the diagnosis. If you cannot fill in where you will play because the team is still arguing about what is wrong, use the kernel instead.

bundles.default_format_guidance: Reach for the kernel when the hard part is that nobody agrees what the problem is. Diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent action force the obstacle to be named before any choice is made, which is why it is the default: the most common defect in a strategy document is that it never says what makes the goal hard.
bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action, and what that rules out) when a team that already shares the context needs to settle what to work on; four sections is enough to end the argument and be cited later. Use full when the strategy has to survive people who were not in the room: it adds who the strategy is and is not for, a falsifiable way to tell whether it is working, the assumptions it would die without, and an event that brings the team back to it. Full is also the right size when the strategy will be handed to an incoming leader, read alongside a funding decision, or used to decline something expensive.
bundles.summary: The document that says which problems this product will solve to reach its vision, and which it will not. It is judged by whether a competitor's name could be swapped in without the document becoming false: a strategy nobody could disagree with has not chosen anything.
bundles.title: Product Strategy

additional_formats.guidance: Reach for the narrative when the vision has to persuade rather than orient: a hiring conversation, a board, a team that has lost the thread. It is the form Marty Cagan argues for and the one he says a canvas cannot reach, because a filled grid states a future while prose can make someone want it.

Reach for the PR/FAQ when the argument is about whether the future is worth having at all. Writing the launch announcement first, dated years out, forces the benefit to be stated in customer language before any engineering path exists, and the FAQ forces the objections into the open while they are still cheap.

bundles.default_format_guidance: Reach for the canvas when the job is to orient people fast and give them something citable: a filled grid can be read in a minute, argued with in a meeting, and quoted back when someone proposes work that does not serve it. It is the form most teams expect, and it is the one Marty Cagan argues is insufficient on its own, which is why the other two exist rather than replacing it.
bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean (the vision, who it is for and what they need, why us, and what it rules out) when a small team needs a shared destination it can actually cite in a prioritisation argument; four sections is enough to do that job. Use full when the vision has to survive contact with people who were not in the room: it adds the competitive context that explains why this future is not already someone else's, the business goals that keep it from being borrowed grandeur, an explicit horizon with a review trigger so it cannot quietly become wallpaper, and the leaps of faith it rests on. Full is also the right size when the vision will be handed to an incoming leader, cited in a funding conversation, or used to justify saying no to something expensive.
bundles.summary: The document that says what future this product is trying to create, for whom, and why this team is the one to build it. It is judged not by how it reads but by whether it can be used to refuse something: a vision nobody has ever cited to say no is decoration.
bundles.title: Product Vision

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean (purpose and scope, the four quadrant tables, review and ownership) for one team on one project, often as a single combined table. Use full when a larger or multi-team program needs richer per-quadrant fields, a steering-group escalation-and-aging view, or cross-quadrant migration tracking; full adds those two sections and splits naturally onto four tabs.
bundles.summary: One working document that tracks the four kinds of open item on a project: Risks (might happen), Assumptions (believed true without proof), Issues (have happened), and Dependencies (structural relationships). A standing governance instrument whose value is the consolidated view - seeing an assumption become an issue, or a dependency become a risk - and whose defining failure is being set up at kickoff and never reviewed.
bundles.title: RAID Log

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean for a routine release; use full for a major launch with breaking changes, migration steps, and audience-specific sections.
bundles.summary: Communicates what changed in a release to users and stakeholders, so people know what is new, what to do, and what to watch for.
bundles.title: Release Notes

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean for a focused, low-blast-radius proposal; use full for a significant decision that needs goals and non-goals, detailed design, alternatives, and a rollout plan.
bundles.summary: Proposes a change and gathers input before the decision is made: the motivation, the proposal, the alternatives, the trade-offs, the open questions, and a place to record the outcome. The pre-decision counterpart to the ADR, which records a decision after it is made.
bundles.title: Request for Comments

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean (purpose and scope, an anchored scoring scale, the risks table, review and ownership) when one team tracks and acts on its own risks. Use full when a steering committee, auditor, or board consumes the register, when you must demonstrate control effectiveness (which needs inherent-vs-residual scoring), or when regulation prescribes fields; full adds dual scoring, escalation and risk appetite, and a closed/materialized audit trail.
bundles.summary: The single, maintained record of the risks to an objective: what could happen, how likely and how damaging, who owns it, the response, and whether that response is working. A standing governance instrument, scored against anchored scales and reviewed on a cadence, that survives the "risk theater" and heat-map critiques by staying living, owned, and objective-anchored.
bundles.title: Risk Register

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean, the Google-style five-section mini design doc, for most changes worth a design doc at all; use full when the design is hard to reverse, crosses teams, or has real non-functional targets, which adds the structural, runtime, interface, and deployment views plus quality attributes and risks.
bundles.summary: Describes how a system will be built: the technical design, its structure, the alternatives weighed, and the cross-cutting concerns, so the design can be reviewed before the code exists. Describes an implementation, as distinct from an RFC (which proposes a decision) and an ADR (which records one).
bundles.title: Software Design Document

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean (Sprint Goal, Selected Items, Delivery Plan) for most sprints; use full when the team is still calibrating its capacity, the forecast and tracking must be legible beyond the team, or the sprint carries real dependencies and carry-over risk, which adds capacity and forecast, progress and tracking, and risks and carry-over.
bundles.summary: The Developers' living plan for a single Sprint: the Sprint Goal (why), the Product Backlog items selected for it (what), and the plan for delivering them (how). A forecast, not a contract; the one thing committed to is the Sprint Goal. Drawn as a Sprint-sized subset from the product backlog.
bundles.title: Sprint Backlog

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean (identification and traceability, preconditions and test data, steps and expected results, postconditions and teardown) for everyday cases written and run by one team; a test case is written hundreds of times over a project, so every extra field is paid for hundreds of times. Use full when the work is regulated or audited, when cases are reviewed as artifacts rather than just executed, when the case is configuration-sensitive, or when the suite is large enough that knowing why a case exists is what lets you retire it; full adds design rationale, environment and configuration, automation status, and version and approval.
bundles.summary: The specification of one verification: what must be true before it runs, what is done, and what must happen as a result, written so that someone who is not its author can ask the same question tomorrow and get the same answer. A design artifact, not a record of a run: it carries no actual result and no pass or fail.
bundles.title: Test Case

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean (scope and non-scope, a risk-ranked approach, entry and exit criteria, environment and ownership, schedule and deliverables) when one team verifies one feature or release. Use full when the work is regulated or audited, when several teams or vendors test the same release, when a formal gate sits inside the cycle, or when your process requires an approved artifact; full adds test levels and types, suspension and resumption criteria, risks to the test effort, and approvals with change control.
bundles.summary: The prospective document that scopes and prioritizes a testing effort: what is being tested and what is explicitly not, which areas carry the most product risk and therefore earn the deepest coverage, the measurable conditions that start and end the work, and who runs it where. Written to be read, not to be complete: the plan is the thinking, not the page count.
bundles.title: Test Plan

bundles.sizing_guidance: Use lean for a single, well-understood story; use full when the story needs detailed context, edge cases, and explicit non-functional notes.
bundles.summary: Describes a unit of work from the user's perspective ("as a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit]") so a team can build and verify the right thing.
bundles.title: User Story
